subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for November 15, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion ta
sentences: Story 1 is about Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion targets in septic shock: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Journal of critical care.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Critically ill or ICU-relevant patients described in the abstract; confirm eligibility criteria in the full text., how should we interpret uncertain. We aimed to evaluate whether these strategies reduce 28/30-day mortality and improve other clinical outcomes compared with usual care. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using a random-effects model wa?
Five RCTs involving 2180 patients with septic shock were included.

Compared with conventional strategies, RSIPPT were not associated with significant differences in 28/30-day mortality (four RCTs; RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.09; I2 = 10%; moderate CoE) or 90-day mortality (three RCTs; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83-1.05; I2 = 0%; low CoE).
However, RSIPPT were associated with fluid reduction during the first 6-8 h of resuscitation (three RCTs; MD -264.53 mL, 95% CI -425.28 to -103.77; I2 = 1%; low CoE).
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.

The bedside implication is this: Potentially practice-relevant because a patient-centered outcome is reported; check absolute risk difference, adverse events, and whether your ICU population matches the study.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

sentences: Story 3 is about Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study..
This is a cohort study from Critical care medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in Critically ill or ICU-relevant patients described in the abstract; confirm eligibility criteria in the full text., how should we interpret l Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated?

During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes.

We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale.
We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.
The bedside implication is this: Useful for risk stratification and hypothesis generation, but avoid causal bedside changes unless supported by interventional evidence.

script.heading: Outro
sentences: That wraps up today's journal club style update.
Before applying any finding, check the full source, the absolute effect size, and your local ICU context.
For English practice, repeat one academic phrase from each article out loud.

articles.title: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.summary: Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes. During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis.
